CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 133 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/31/2026 - PAGE 1 OF 3




           BEFORE THE CORPORATION COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA

          IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF                           )
          OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY                             ) Case No. PUD2026-000031
          FOR COMMISSION APPROVAL OF ELECTRIC                           )
          SERVICE AGREEMENTS AND PREAPPROVAL                            )
          OF CAPACITY PURCHASE AGREEMENTS                               )
          PURSUANT TO 17 O.S. § 286(C)                                  )

                      Redacted Confidential Testimony Summary of Matthew DeCourcey

         Direct Testimony

                  In his Direct Testimony, Matthew DeCourcey first provides his educational qualifications
         and employment history. He has previously appeared before the Oklahoma Corporation
         Commission in PUD 2021-00163 on behalf of Empire District and has made appearances before
         utility regulators in other jurisdictions. Mr. DeCourcey explained the purpose of his testimony is
         to support OG&E’s request to approve the Electric Service Agreements, or ESAs, it has executed
         with Alliance Site and Grid, LLC, a subsidiary of Google Energy, LLC, to serve new data centers.

                  Mr. DeCourcey testified that an industry standard has emerged requiring utilities seeking
         to serve new large load customers to demonstrate two types of protection for existing customers:
         protection from the risk of stranded costs and protection from cost subsidies (i.e., existing
         customers paying a portion of the costs to serve new large load customers). He explained that
         stranded costs arise when a utility makes investments to serve a customer that subsequently leaves
         the system, leaving unrecovered costs that other customers would potentially need to absorb. He
         noted that regulators in Indiana, Nevada, Ohio, Missouri, Michigan, and other states have
         investigated and implemented large load tariffs, and that policymakers including the Trump White
         House, through its Ratepayer Protection Pledge issued in March 2026, have emphasized these
         same priorities and have sought to protect existing utility customers from stranded cost risks and
         from subsidizing the costs of serving new large loads. He further noted that Alphabet, the parent
         company of Google, is a signatory to that pledge. He stated that where utilities have demonstrated
         adequate customer protections, regulators have generally approved special contracts and large load
         tariffs. He also noted that the Staff of the Public Utilities Division has identified stranded cost risk
         and cost subsidy prevention as key regulatory issues that must resolved before integrating new
         large loads, consistent with his own conclusions.

                 Mr. DeCourcey then testified that the ESAs effectively mitigate the risk of stranded costs
         through multiple contractual mechanisms. He explained that the ESAs require Google to fund
         100% of the costs of dedicated transmission and distribution infrastructure through a Contribution
         in Aid of Construction, impose a
                                                                   , and establish an exit fee calculated by
         applying the     contract minimum for the entire duration of the agreement. He further explained
         that the ESAs include a unique energy-based minimum billing requirement based on                 of
         energy charges assuming an         load factor to the minimum demand requirement, and require

         Google to provide credit equal to the entire remaining value of the contract, effectively pre-funding
         the exit fee and eliminating default risk. He compared these provisions against large load tariffs
         approved for eleven other utilities, including AEP Ohio, Ameren Missouri, Appalachian Power,
         Consumers Energy, Evergy Kansas, Florida Power and Light, Indiana Michigan Power, Kentucky
         Power, PPL Electric, Santee Cooper, and Virginia Electric Power Company, and concluded that
         the ESAs meet or exceed the protections in place at each. He also reviewed recently approved and
         pending special contracts, including the DTE-Oracle agreement in Michigan and the WPL-Degas
         agreement in Wisconsin, and found that neither provides more robust customer protections than
         the ESAs.

                 Mr. DeCourcey further testified that existing customers will not subsidize OG&E’s cost to
         serve Google’s loads and that rates for existing customers are likely to decline. He referenced the
         Cost of Service Study conducted by Company Witness Jason Thenmadathil, which updated the
         COSS approved in OG&E’s last base rate case to include demand from the new data centers and
         found that adding the new loads will shift costs away from other customer classes and toward
         Google. He stated that this finding is consistent with conclusions reached by utilities and
         regulators in other jurisdictions, citing examples from Michigan, Georgia Power, Evergy, and
         Pacific Gas and Electric. Georgia Power, for example, estimated cost savings of at least $8.50 per
         month for residential customers in 2029, 2030, and 2031, and PG&E claimed that for every 1,000
         MW of demand added under its proposed tariff, total costs for existing customers will decline by
         1-2%.

                  Mr. DeCourcey testified that the ESAs establish a powerful fail-safe mechanism that
         facilitates the Commission’s after-the-fact review of customer benefits and impacts from adding
         Google as an OG&E customer. He explained that the parties have acknowledged that the
         Commission can review potential rate impacts without limitation on what a potential impact might
         consist of, that such reviews would be conducted on an ex-post basis using financial actuals rather
         than forecasts, and that the Commission will have frequent opportunities to review impacts in each
         general rate case proceeding and each review proceeding for the Company’s Fuel Cost Adjustment
         rider. He stated that he is not aware of any other mechanisms structured in exactly this way and
         that on the basis of the fail-safe mechanism alone, it would be reasonable to characterize these
         agreements as being very much oriented towards protecting OG&E’s existing customers. He also
         noted that OG&E is developing a large load tariff that could provide additional customer
         protections, and that Google will pay rates under the rate tariffs applicable to it. For these reasons,
         Mr. DeCourcey concluded by recommending that the Commission approve the Company’s
         Application.
